name: France
description:
**France** is the reference point against which most of the wine world measures itself, home to the grapes, styles, and place-based thinking that the rest of the industry has borrowed for centuries. It rivals Italy as the largest producer by volume, but its lasting influence comes from how tightly it links a wine to the exact patch of ground it grew on.

**Signature wines** — the classics: age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot blends from Bordeaux, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Burgundy, the sparkling benchmark of Champagne, Syrah and Grenache in the Rhône, and crisp Sauvignon Blanc and Chenin Blanc in the Loire.

**Key regions** — Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne, the Rhône Valley, the Loire Valley, Alsace, Beaujolais, and Provence.

**Good to know** — France pioneered the appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC) system in the 1930s, a legal framework that ties allowed grapes, yields, and methods to defined geographic zones. The Burgundian idea of terroir — that soil, slope, and climate shape a wine's identity — originates here and now underpins fine wine everywhere.

name: Italy
description:
**Italy** is one of the world's largest and most diverse wine producers, with grapevines grown in every one of its regions from the Alps to Sicily. Its great strength is an astonishing library of native grape varieties, giving it a range of flavours and styles matched by few other countries.

**Signature wines** — Sangiovese-based reds like Chianti and Brunello, the powerful Nebbiolo of Barolo and Barbaresco, juicy Montepulciano and rich Primitivo in the south, plus sparkling Prosecco (Glera) and countless distinctive whites.

**Key regions** — Tuscany, Piedmont, the Veneto, and further afield Sicily, Puglia, Campania, Friuli, and Trentino-Alto Adige.

**Good to know** — Italy's quality tiers run from IGT up through DOC to the top DOCG designation, though some of its most celebrated wines, the so-called Super Tuscans, deliberately sat outside the traditional rules when they first appeared. With hundreds of indigenous varieties still in commercial use, Italy offers more genuine diversity than almost anywhere else.

name: United States
description:
**United States** is the largest wine producer outside Europe and a major force in the global market, with California alone accounting for the overwhelming majority of its output. American wine ranges from mass-market bottlings to some of the most sought-after cult wines in the world.

**Signature wines** — bold Cabernet Sauvignon and Zinfandel, ripe Chardonnay, and cool-climate Pinot Noir; Washington and Oregon add elegant reds and aromatic whites to the picture.

**Key regions** — California (Napa Valley, Sonoma, Paso Robles, and beyond), Oregon's Willamette Valley, and Washington's Columbia Valley, with growing scenes in New York's Finger Lakes and elsewhere.

**Good to know** — the US uses the American Viticultural Area (AVA) system to define grape-growing zones by geography, though unlike Europe it does not dictate which grapes may be planted or how wine must be made. The 1976 "Judgment of Paris" tasting, where California wines bested French classics in a blind lineup, put American wine firmly on the world stage.

name: Germany
description:
**Germany** is one of the world's great white wine countries and the spiritual home of Riesling, producing wines of remarkable purity, acidity, and ageing potential from some of the coolest vineyards in Europe. Its steep river valleys yield wines that balance featherlight delicacy with intense flavour.

**Signature wines** — Riesling above all, in styles from bone-dry (trocken) to lusciously sweet, alongside increasingly serious Pinot Noir (known here as Spätburgunder) and other Pinot family whites like Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder.

**Key regions** — the Mosel, the Rheingau, the Pfalz, Rheinhessen, the Nahe, and Baden.

**Good to know** — German wine labels traditionally grade quality by grape ripeness at harvest, using the Prädikat scale that runs from Kabinett through Spätlese and Auslese up to the rare, sweet Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese. This ripeness ladder means a single vineyard can produce everything from a crisp dry wine to an unctuous dessert wine depending on when the grapes are picked.

name: New Zealand
description:
**New Zealand** is a small wine country with an outsized reputation, famous for putting a bright, pungent style of Sauvignon Blanc on the global map in a single generation. Its cool, maritime climate and long ripening season give the wines vivid aromatics and racy acidity.

**Signature wines** — zesty, passionfruit-and-herb Sauvignon Blanc above all, plus elegant Pinot Noir, refined Chardonnay, and aromatic whites like Pinot Gris and Riesling.

**Key regions** — Marlborough (the Sauvignon Blanc heartland), Central Otago and Martinborough for Pinot Noir, plus Hawke's Bay, Nelson, and Gisborne.

**Good to know** — New Zealand's wine industry is remarkably young, having exploded from a handful of producers in the 1970s and 80s into a globally recognised name, driven largely by Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc. Its distance from other wine regions and strict biosecurity have kept many vineyard pests at bay, and the country is a leader in sustainable growing practices.

name: Australia
description:
**Australia** is a major New World wine power, known for warm, generous, fruit-driven wines and a pioneering, technically confident approach to winemaking. It spans everything from vast, value-focused production to small estates crafting some of the Southern Hemisphere's most celebrated bottles.

**Signature wines** — rich, spicy Shiraz above all, alongside Cabernet Sauvignon, buttery-to-refined Chardonnay, and increasingly Grenache blends and cool-climate Riesling.

**Key regions** — the Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale for Shiraz, Coonawarra for Cabernet, the Hunter Valley, Margaret River in the west, the Yarra Valley, Clare and Eden Valleys for Riesling, and Tasmania for sparkling and cool-climate wines.

**Good to know** — Australia uses a Geographical Indication system to define its wine zones, though labelling revolves more around grape variety than strict regional rules. Some of its oldest vineyards, particularly in the Barossa, survived the phylloxera louse that devastated Europe, giving the country access to genuinely ancient, ungrafted vines.

name: Spain
description:
**Spain** has more land under vine than any other country and a winemaking tradition stretching back thousands of years, offering exceptional value alongside a growing tier of world-class wines. Its dry, sunny climate and wealth of native grapes give it a character all its own.

**Signature wines** — Tempranillo-based reds from Rioja and Ribera del Duero, powerful Garnacha (Grenache), the sparkling Cava, the fortified wines of Jerez (Sherry), and crisp Albariño whites from the Atlantic northwest.

**Key regions** — Rioja, Ribera del Duero, Priorat, Rías Baixas, Jerez, Rueda, and Penedès.

**Good to know** — Spain's quality system runs from the broad DO category up to the prestigious DOCa/DOQ tier, held only by Rioja and Priorat. Many Spanish reds are also classified by ageing, with terms like Crianza, Reserva, and Gran Reserva on the label indicating how long a wine spent maturing in barrel and bottle before release.

name: South Africa
description:
**South Africa** bridges the Old and New Worlds, combining centuries of winemaking history with a modern, quality-focused revival that has drawn growing international attention. Its vineyards, cooled by Atlantic breezes and shaped by ancient soils, produce wines of freshness and increasing finesse.

**Signature wines** — Chenin Blanc (locally its most-planted white, once called Steen), the country's own Pinotage red, plus Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Chardonnay, and Sauvignon Blanc.

**Key regions** — Stellenbosch, Paarl, Franschhoek, Constantia, Swartland, and Walker Bay, most clustered in the Western Cape.

**Good to know** — winemaking at the Cape dates back to the mid-1600s, and the historic Constantia sweet wines were prized by European nobility long ago. Pinotage, a crossing of Pinot Noir and Cinsault created here in the 1920s, is the country's signature homegrown grape, and the Swartland region has become a hotbed for a new wave of ambitious, low-intervention producers.

name: Portugal
description:
**Portugal** punches far above its size, a small Atlantic country with an extraordinary trove of native grapes and one of the oldest demarcated wine regions on earth. It is famous worldwide for fortified Port and Madeira, but its dry table wines have surged in reputation and value.

**Signature wines** — Port and Madeira above all, plus rich dry reds from Touriga Nacional and blends, crisp low-alcohol Vinho Verde whites, and characterful whites and reds from indigenous varieties found almost nowhere else.

**Key regions** — the Douro Valley (source of Port and increasingly serious dry reds), the Dão and Bairrada for structured wines, Vinho Verde in the green northwest, the warm Alentejo for approachable reds, and the island of Madeira.

**Good to know** — Portugal's tiered system runs from the top DOC/DOP down through regional (Vinho Regional) labels. The Douro was formally demarcated in 1756, making it one of the world's first protected wine appellations, and the country still relies heavily on hundreds of local grapes rather than international ones.

name: Argentina
description:
**Argentina** is South America's largest wine producer and one of the New World's most recognizable, defined by high-altitude vineyards climbing toward the Andes and a signature red that became its calling card. Once inward-looking, it now exports its style with confidence.

**Signature wines** — bold, plush Malbec is the flagship, giving deeply colored reds with ripe dark fruit; the aromatic white Torrontés is the distinctive native counterpart, alongside solid Cabernet Sauvignon and Bonarda.

**Key regions** — Mendoza dominates production and includes prized sub-zones like the Uco Valley and Luján de Cuyo; further north Salta grows vines at some of the world's highest elevations, while Patagonia in the south offers a cooler, fresher profile.

**Good to know** — Argentine wine country is essentially high desert, irrigated by Andean snowmelt, and altitude does much of the work that latitude does elsewhere, keeping acidity and color intense under strong sunlight. Malbec, though French in origin, found its truest home here.

name: Canada
description:
**Canada** is a cool-climate wine country best known internationally for one specialty: intensely sweet, concentrated Icewine made from grapes frozen on the vine. Beyond that headline, it produces increasingly respected dry table and sparkling wines from a handful of provinces.

**Signature wines** — Icewine, most famously from Vidal and Riesling but also red Cabernet Franc; alongside it, crisp Rieslings, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, and traditional-method sparkling wines.

**Key regions** — Ontario's Niagara Peninsula, moderated by the Great Lakes, and British Columbia's Okanagan Valley are the two heavyweights, with smaller pockets in Nova Scotia and elsewhere.

**Good to know** — Canada's VQA (Vintners Quality Alliance) system certifies origin and standards, and its Icewine rules are strict: grapes must be naturally frozen and pressed while still frozen, which is why cold-winter Canada became the world's most reliable large-scale producer of the style.

name: Austria
description:
**Austria** is a benchmark cool-climate country producing precise, food-friendly wines with a strong dry-white identity and a serious quality reputation rebuilt over recent decades. Production is modest in scale but consistently high in standard.

**Signature wines** — Grüner Veltliner, the peppery, versatile white that is the national signature, and racy Rieslings lead the way; among reds, Blaufränkisch and Zweigelt give firm, spicy, distinctly central-European styles. Sweet wines from Burgenland are also renowned.

**Key regions** — the Wachau, Kremstal, and Kamptal along the Danube for top whites; Burgenland near the Hungarian border for reds and lusciously sweet wines; and Styria (Steiermark) in the south for aromatic whites.

**Good to know** — Austria overhauled its wine law after a 1980s adulteration scandal, emerging with some of Europe's strictest standards. The Wachau uses its own tiered ripeness categories (Steinfeder, Federspiel, Smaragd), and much of the country's identity rests on dry, transparent, terroir-driven whites.

name: Chile
description:
**Chile** is one of the New World's most reliable and export-focused wine countries, blessed with a long, narrow geography squeezed between the Andes and the Pacific that gives it remarkable range and a naturally healthy vineyard environment. It offers strong value across every price tier.

**Signature wines** — Cabernet Sauvignon and Bordeaux-style reds are the backbone, but Carménère, a nearly lost Bordeaux grape rediscovered here, has become Chile's signature; Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, and Syrah round out the range.

**Key regions** — the Central Valley (including Maipo, the Rapel Valley with its renowned Colchagua, and Maule) for reds, cooler coastal zones like Casablanca and San Antonio for whites and Pinot Noir, and the northern Limarí and Elqui valleys.

**Good to know** — Chile's isolation, bounded by desert, ocean, mountains, and ice, kept the vine louse phylloxera out, so many vines grow on their own ungrafted roots. Carménère was long mistaken for Merlot until identified in the 1990s.

name: Greece
description:
**Greece** has one of the longest continuous winemaking histories in the world, stretching back thousands of years, and today it is celebrated for a wealth of distinctive indigenous grapes that exist almost nowhere else. Its modern revival has turned it into a favorite of curious drinkers.

**Signature wines** — the crisp, mineral white Assyrtiko, grown famously on volcanic Santorini, is the flagship; reds from Xinomavro and Agiorgitiko show structure and character; Moschofilero and Malagousia add aromatic whites, and sweet Vinsanto and Mavrodaphne complete the picture.

**Key regions** — the volcanic island of Santorini, Naoussa and Amyndeon in the north for Xinomavro, Nemea in the Peloponnese for Agiorgitiko, plus Crete, Macedonia, and other islands.

**Good to know** — Greece uses the EU's PDO/PGI framework for its appellations. Retsina, the resin-flavored white, is its most famous export cliché, but the real story now is serious dry wine from native varieties, with Santorini's ancient basket-trained, ungrafted vines a particular treasure.

name: Switzerland
description:
**Switzerland** is a small, high-quality producer whose wines are rarely seen abroad because the Swiss drink almost all of it themselves. Alpine and lakeside vineyards, often on dramatic terraces, yield fresh, precise wines shaped by three cultural influences.

**Signature wines** — the white Chasselas is the national specialty, giving delicate, mineral, lightly aromatic wines; among reds, Pinot Noir and Gamay are widespread, and the Valais grows an array of rare local grapes such as Petite Arvine and Cornalin.

**Key regions** — the French-speaking Valais and Vaud along the Rhône and Lake Geneva account for most production, with the Italian-speaking Ticino specializing in Merlot and German-speaking cantons focused on Pinot Noir.

**Good to know** — winegrowing here spans French, German, and Italian linguistic zones, each with its own grapes and traditions. The steep Lavaux terraces above Lake Geneva are a UNESCO World Heritage site, and Swiss production is dominated by tiny plots and boutique volumes.

name: Sweden
description:
**Sweden** is an emerging cool-climate wine country in the far north of Europe, where commercial winegrowing is young and small in scale but slowly expanding as the climate warms and hardy grape varieties improve. Expect fresh, light, high-acid styles rather than power.

**Signature wines** — crisp whites and sparkling wines are the natural fit, typically made from cold-hardy hybrid and early-ripening varieties such as Solaris, alongside experiments with Pinot Noir and other cool-climate grapes for light reds and rosés.

**Key regions** — plantings cluster in the milder south, particularly Skåne, along with vineyards on the island of Öland and around the country's southern lakes and coasts, where the sea moderates temperatures.

**Good to know** — Sweden falls under the EU wine framework, and although the industry is still tiny and largely artisanal, a growing number of boutique estates have shown that quality sparkling and aromatic white wine is genuinely achievable at this latitude.

name: Mexico
description:
**Mexico** is the oldest wine-producing country in the Americas, with vines planted by Spanish colonists in the 1500s, though for centuries the industry was overshadowed by beer, spirits and a colonial ban on new plantings. Today it is a small but ambitious producer whose modern quality revival has drawn real international attention.

**Signature wines** — Bold reds are the calling card, from Nebbiolo, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache and Tempranillo, often in warm, ripe, sun-driven styles, alongside a growing range of whites and rosés.

**Key regions** — The Valle de Guadalupe in Baja California is the heart of quality wine, cooled by Pacific breezes; other pockets exist in Coahuila, Querétaro and Zacatecas at high altitude.

**Good to know** — Mexico has no elaborate national appellation hierarchy in the European sense, and much of its output is concentrated in Baja. The country also grows enormous quantities of grapes for brandy, which historically defined its viticulture more than table wine.

name: England
description:
**England** has transformed from a fringe curiosity into one of the wine world's most talked-about newcomers, driven above all by sparkling wine. A cool, marginal climate that was long a handicap has become an asset as warming temperatures let grapes ripen more reliably.

**Signature wines** — Traditional-method sparkling wine made from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier — the same trio as Champagne — is the flagship, prized for its bright acidity and finesse; still wines, especially from Bacchus, are a growing sideline.

**Key regions** — The southern counties dominate, particularly Sussex, Kent and Hampshire, where chalk soils echo those of Champagne, with further plantings in Surrey and beyond.

**Good to know** — England shares a geological chalk seam with the Champagne region across the Channel, which helps explain the affinity. Sussex has been granted its own protected designation, a sign of the industry's growing maturity and confidence.

name: Croatia
description:
**Croatia** is a historic Mediterranean and Central European wine country with a viticultural past stretching back to antiquity, and a wealth of indigenous grape varieties that give its wines a distinct local character. Production is small in global terms but deeply rooted in regional identity.

**Signature wines** — Along the Adriatic coast, the powerful red Plavac Mali stands out, a relative of Zinfandel; inland and on the Istrian peninsula, the crisp white Graševina (Welschriesling) and the aromatic Malvazija Istarska are widely grown.

**Key regions** — The Dalmatian coast and its islands produce concentrated reds; Istria in the northwest is known for fresh whites and food-friendly styles; the continental interior around Slavonia yields much of the country's white wine.

**Good to know** — DNA research famously traced California's Zinfandel back to an old Croatian variety (Tribidrag/Crljenak Kaštelanski), confirming a link that had long been suspected between the Adriatic coast and the New World grape.

name: Hungary
description:
**Hungary** is one of Central Europe's great wine nations, with a proud tradition anchored by Tokaji, one of the world's most celebrated sweet wines. It offers a broad and often underrated range across sweet, dry white and red styles, built on a deep bench of native grapes.

**Signature wines** — Sweet Tokaji Aszú, made from botrytis-affected (nobly rotted) grapes led by Furmint and Hárslevelű, is the crown jewel; increasingly, dry Furmint shows the same terroir in a different guise. Robust reds come from Kékfrankos (Blaufränkisch) and the blended Bull's Blood.

**Key regions** — Tokaj in the northeast is the historic sweet-wine heartland; Eger and Villány are known for reds; Somló and Badacsony produce distinctive volcanic-soil whites.

**Good to know** — Tokaji was cherished by European royal courts and was one of the first wine regions in the world to be classified, well before Bordeaux's famous ranking, marking Hungary as a pioneer of appellation thinking.

name: Japan
description:
**Japan** is a small, quality-focused wine producer whose reputation has grown quickly, celebrated for delicate, precise wines suited to the country's cuisine. Winemaking dates to the late 19th century, but the modern serious industry is a more recent story of dedication in a challenging, humid climate.

**Signature wines** — The native pink-skinned grape Koshu makes light, subtle, low-alcohol white wines with gentle citrus and a clean finish; Muscat Bailey A, a hybrid, produces soft, fragrant reds. International varieties are also grown.

**Key regions** — Yamanashi Prefecture, west of Tokyo, is the historic center and Koshu's home; Nagano, Hokkaido and Yamagata are important cooler-climate areas gaining recognition.

**Good to know** — The term "Japan Wine" is legally protected to mean wine made from domestically grown grapes, distinguishing it from the many blends historically bottled in Japan using imported bulk wine or concentrate. Koshu itself is a grape of ancient Eurasian origin adapted over centuries to Japanese conditions.

name: Georgia
description:
**Georgia** is widely regarded as one of the cradles of winemaking, with an unbroken tradition reaching back some 8,000 years — likely the oldest continuous wine culture on Earth. It is a country where wine is woven into national identity, religion and daily life.

**Signature wines** — The white grape Rkatsiteli and the red Saperavi are the pillars; Saperavi is a deeply colored, structured red, notable as a rare teinturier grape with red flesh as well as red skin. Amber (orange) skin-contact whites are a hallmark.

**Key regions** — Kakheti in the east is the dominant region, producing the majority of Georgia's wine, with other pockets in Kartli, Imereti and the far west.

**Good to know** — Traditional Georgian wine is fermented and aged in large egg-shaped clay vessels called qvevri, buried underground; this ancient method is recognized by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage and inspired the modern natural and orange wine movements.

name: Lebanon
description:
**Lebanon** is one of the world's most historic wine regions, heir to Phoenician traders who spread viticulture across the ancient Mediterranean. Despite decades of conflict, its winemakers have kept producing, and the country enjoys a reputation well beyond its modest size.

**Signature wines** — Full-bodied reds dominate, typically Bordeaux and Rhône blends of Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Grenache, Cinsault and Carignan, ripe and warming in style; whites and the native Merwah and Obeidi grapes round out the range.

**Key regions** — The high-altitude Bekaa Valley, sitting well above sea level between two mountain ranges, is the center of production, its elevation tempering the Mediterranean heat.

**Good to know** — French influence runs deep from the colonial era, shaping grape choices and a Bordeaux-leaning style. Some Lebanese estates trace their history to the 19th century and have become internationally admired symbols of resilience and quality.

name: Netherlands
description:
**Netherlands** is a small and emerging wine country whose cool, maritime northern climate has historically made grape growing difficult. A warming climate and disease-resistant hybrid grapes have driven a modest but genuine expansion of domestic vineyards in recent years.

**Signature wines** — Much of the output relies on cool-climate and hybrid varieties such as Solaris, Souvignier Gris, Regent and Johanniter, yielding mostly fresh whites and some sparkling and light red wines.

**Key regions** — Plantings are scattered across the southern and eastern provinces, notably Limburg and Gelderland, where slightly warmer, more sheltered sites give grapes a better chance to ripen.

**Good to know** — The Dutch have a far larger place in wine history as merchants than as growers: in the 17th century they were dominant traders who helped shape styles across Europe, from Bordeaux to sweet wines, long before they made much wine of their own.

name: Belgium
description:
**Belgium** is a small, cool-climate wine producer better known abroad for its beer, but its vineyards have grown steadily as warming conditions make grape ripening more reliable.

**Signature wines** — crisp whites and traditional-method sparkling wines dominate, made from cool-climate grapes such as Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and aromatic varieties; some hybrid grapes are also grown for hardiness.

**Key regions** — production is concentrated in Flanders, with areas like Hageland and Haspengouw among the recognised zones, plus scattered vineyards in Wallonia.

**Good to know** — Belgium operates within the EU quality framework, with several protected designations of origin covering both still and sparkling wine. Sparkling wine in particular has become a point of pride, and warmer seasons have made ripe, dependable vintages steadily easier to achieve.

name: Serbia
description:
**Serbia** has a long and deep winemaking tradition in the Balkans, disrupted by the twentieth century but now enjoying a confident revival driven by small family estates and a renewed focus on native grapes.

**Signature wines** — the country is best known for reds from the indigenous Prokupac grape, alongside aromatic whites from Tamjanika (a Muscat relative); international varieties are also widely planted.

**Key regions** — notable areas include Fruška Gora in the north, Šumadija in the central heartland, and the Negotin region near the Danube in the east.

**Good to know** — winemaking here dates back to Roman times, and Serbia sits within the broader historical wine belt of southeastern Europe. Modern producers have leaned into reviving heritage varieties as a way to distinguish Serbian wine on the international market.

name: Turkey
description:
**Turkey** has one of the oldest continuous grape-growing histories on earth, though much of its enormous crop goes to table grapes and raisins; wine is a smaller but increasingly interesting share, powered by a treasury of native grapes.

**Signature wines** — indigenous varieties define the best bottles: reds from Öküzgözü and Boğazkere in the east, the softer Kalecik Karası in central Anatolia, and whites from Narince and the high-altitude Emir grape.

**Key regions** — key zones include Thrace near the European frontier, the Aegean coast, and central Anatolia, including the volcanic landscape of Cappadocia.

**Good to know** — vines have been cultivated across Anatolia for thousands of years, making it part of the ancestral homeland of the wine grape. Today a handful of ambitious producers channel that heritage into modern, export-minded wines despite a challenging domestic market.

name: Morocco
description:
**Morocco** is one of North Africa's more established wine producers, with a warm Mediterranean climate tempered by Atlantic breezes and altitude, and a wine culture shaped heavily by its French colonial period.

**Signature wines** — reds and rosés lead, most famously the pale, dry "vin gris" style; French grapes such as Grenache, Cinsault, Carignan and Syrah are widely planted.

**Key regions** — the vineyards around Meknès and the Guerrouane area, on the plains and foothills inland from the coast, form the country's viticultural core.

**Good to know** — Morocco has a French-style appellation system regulating its top zones. Although it is a Muslim-majority country where domestic consumption is limited, its wines find a steady export audience, particularly in France.

name: Kazakhstan
description:
**Kazakhstan** is an emerging Central Asian wine producer with a modest but growing industry, drawing on a grape-growing tradition that predates and outlasted the Soviet era.

**Signature wines** — the country makes both reds and whites, using a mix of international varieties and hardy grapes suited to its continental climate of hot summers and cold winters.

**Key regions** — production is concentrated in the warmer south and southeast, notably around Almaty and the foothills near the border with Central Asian neighbours.

**Good to know** — this part of Central Asia lies close to the ancient dispersal routes of the cultivated grapevine, giving the region a genuine, if under-documented, place in wine history. Modern investment has begun to lift quality, though the industry remains small on the world stage.

name: Lithuania
description:
**Lithuania** is a Baltic country on the cold northern margin of grape growing, where wine production is very small and challenging owing to short, cool seasons.

**Signature wines** — historically much "wine" here has meant fruit and berry wine rather than grape wine; where grapes are grown, cold-hardy hybrid varieties suited to a harsh continental climate are the norm.

**Key regions** — vineyards are few and scattered, tended largely by hobbyists and small enthusiasts rather than a formal regional structure.

**Good to know** — as an EU member, Lithuania falls under European wine regulations, but it is not a traditional grape-wine nation. Its drinking culture leans toward beer and spirits, with grape wine remaining a niche, emerging pursuit.

name: Dominican Republic
description:
**Dominican Republic** is a Caribbean nation with only a marginal presence in the wine world, since its hot, humid tropical climate is poorly suited to conventional grape growing.

**Signature wines** — grape-based wine production is minimal; where wines are made, they tend to rely on imported grapes or grape must, and tropical fruit wines are also part of the local picture.

**Key regions** — there is no established fine-wine region, and any viticulture is small-scale and experimental.

**Good to know** — the country is far better known as a producer of rum and as a Caribbean tourism destination than as a wine source. Its inclusion reflects niche and novelty production rather than a recognised winemaking tradition.

name: Armenia
description:
**Armenia** is one of the true cradles of wine, home to some of the earliest known winemaking sites, and today it is enjoying a spirited revival built around its ancient native grapes and high-altitude vineyards.

**Signature wines** — the flagship is red wine from the indigenous Areni grape, prized for its freshness and character; the country also produces distinctive whites and has a strong tradition of brandy.

**Key regions** — the Vayots Dzor region in the south, including the area around the village of Areni, is the most celebrated, with vineyards planted at some of the highest elevations in the world.

**Good to know** — the Areni-1 cave complex yielded evidence of a winery thousands of years old, among the oldest ever discovered, anchoring Armenia's claim to a founding role in wine history. Modern producers have used this deep heritage as the foundation for a growing quality wine sector.

name: Brazil
description:
**Brazil** is South America's third-largest wine producer, and while it lives in the shadow of Argentina and Chile, it has carved out a genuine international reputation, above all for its sparkling wines.

**Signature wines** — Traditional-method and Charmat sparkling wines are the country's calling card, prized for their freshness and value. Still reds and whites are made from the usual international grapes, alongside a long legacy of American hybrids planted by early settlers.

**Key regions** — Serra Gaúcha in the southern state of Rio Grande do Sul is the historic heartland, and within it the Vale dos Vinhedos became the country's first demarcated appellation. Further north, the Vale do São Francisco is a tropical outlier where vines can be coaxed into more than one harvest a year.

**Good to know** — Brazilian viticulture was shaped heavily by Italian immigrants who arrived in the late 19th century, and their descendants still run many of the family wineries. The cool, humid, hilly conditions of the south suit sparkling production far better than they suit big, ripe reds.

name: Bulgaria
description:
**Bulgaria** is one of the oldest wine-growing lands in Europe, with roots reaching back to Thracian antiquity, and in the 1980s it was among the world's largest wine exporters before reinventing itself as a quality-focused producer.

**Signature wines** — The country is best known for reds, both from international grapes like Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot and, increasingly, from characterful native varieties. Mavrud and Melnik give dark, structured, ageworthy reds, while Rubin is a local crossing and Dimyat and Misket supply aromatic whites.

**Key regions** — Winemaking spreads across the Thracian Lowlands, the Danubian Plain, the Black Sea coast, and the warmer valleys of the southwest around Melnik.

**Good to know** — During the communist era, Bulgaria built vast state-run vineyards aimed squarely at export markets, and its inexpensive Cabernet became a familiar sight abroad. Since joining the EU, the industry has shifted toward smaller estates, indigenous grapes, and modern cellars, adopting EU appellation categories in place of the old state system.

name: Czech Republic
description:
**Czech Republic** is a small, mostly white-wine country in Central Europe whose production is concentrated overwhelmingly in the south-eastern corner, and whose wines are largely enjoyed at home rather than exported.

**Signature wines** — Crisp, aromatic whites dominate, made from grapes that reflect the country's Central European neighbourhood: Grüner Veltliner, Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Welschriesling, and Pinot varieties. Light reds and a lively tradition of young, freshly fermented wine round out the picture.

**Key regions** — Moravia (Morava), in the south-east near the Austrian and Slovak borders, accounts for the great majority of vineyards, while Bohemia (Čechy) has a smaller cluster of plantings north of Prague.

**Good to know** — As an EU member, the country follows European quality tiers, with a system of predicate wines graded by grape ripeness at harvest, echoing the Germanic model. A local highlight is *burčák*, the cloudy, still-fermenting partial wine sold for a few weeks each autumn.

name: Israel
description:
**Israel** pairs one of the most ancient winemaking histories on earth with a thoroughly modern industry that was revived in the late 19th century and has surged in quality since the 1980s.

**Signature wines** — Bordeaux grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot lead the reds, joined by Syrah, with Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc among the whites; Mediterranean varieties and revived indigenous grapes are a growing focus. Much of the wine is produced kosher, an option rather than a limitation on style.

**Key regions** — The cooler, higher Galilee and Golan Heights in the north are the most prized zones, alongside the Judean Hills near Jerusalem, the coastal Shomron, and the surprising desert plantings of the Negev.

**Good to know** — The modern industry owes much to Baron Edmond de Rothschild, who backed its founding wineries in the 1880s. Altitude and cooling breezes are the key to quality here, letting growers offset the warmth of the Eastern Mediterranean climate.

name: Luxembourg
description:
**Luxembourg** is a tiny but serious wine producer whose vineyards line the left bank of the Moselle River, making almost exclusively white and sparkling wines of notable crispness.

**Signature wines** — Aromatic, high-acid whites are the specialty, from Riesling, Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc, Auxerrois, Rivaner (the local name for Müller-Thurgau), and the old workhorse Elbling. The country also has a strong traditional-method sparkling tradition.

**Key regions** — Production is confined to a single stretch: the Luxembourg Moselle, a ribbon of steep and gentle slopes running along the German border in the country's south-east.

**Good to know** — Wines qualify for the national *Moselle Luxembourgeoise* appellation, and quality sparkling wine is bottled under the protected *Crémant de Luxembourg* label, made by the same method as Champagne. Given the northerly, cool-climate setting, freshness and delicacy define the house style rather than power.

name: North Macedonia
description:
**North Macedonia** is a small Balkan country with a long viticultural history and a warm, sunny continental climate that favours ripe, generous red wines.

**Signature wines** — The flagship grape is Vranec, which yields deep, full-bodied, tannic reds, often supported by Kratošija and international varieties. Among whites, Smederevka and the aromatic Temjanika are widely grown, and Stanušina is a prized local rarity.

**Key regions** — The Vardar River Valley in the country's centre is the dominant zone, and within it Tikveš is the largest and best-known winegrowing district.

**Good to know** — For much of the 20th century the region supplied bulk wine within the former Yugoslavia, but since independence producers have invested heavily in bottling under their own labels and highlighting native grapes. Warm days and a generous growing season make full-bodied reds the country's natural strength.

name: Norway
description:
**Norway** sits at the very frontier of viticulture, a cold northern country where commercial grape growing is a small and relatively recent experiment rather than an established tradition.

**Signature wines** — The handful of vineyards that exist rely on cold-hardy hybrid grapes bred to ripen in short, cool growing seasons. Alongside these pioneering still wines, Norway has a much larger and well-known tradition of fruit wines made from apples, berries, and other cold-climate produce.

**Key regions** — Plantings are scattered and modest, generally found in the milder, more sheltered pockets of the south where the growing season is longest.

**Good to know** — As climate conditions gradually shift and grape breeding improves, a few determined growers have proven that vines can be ripened this far north, though volumes remain tiny. Norway is best understood as an emerging curiosity at the outer edge of the wine world rather than a producer of scale.

name: Poland
description:
**Poland** is a small, fast-emerging cool-climate wine country where a modest but enthusiastic revival of commercial viticulture has taken hold over the past couple of decades.

**Signature wines** — Growers lean heavily on cold-hardy hybrid grapes such as Solaris and Rondo, which ripen reliably in short northern seasons, alongside increasingly successful plantings of Riesling, Pinot Noir, and other classic varieties in warmer sites. Fresh, light whites and rosés are the natural fit for the climate.

**Key regions** — Vineyards cluster in the country's warmer southern and western belts, including areas around Zielona Góra in the west and the hills of Lesser Poland (Małopolska) in the south.

**Good to know** — Poland once had a longer winegrowing history that faded over the centuries, and today's scene is very much a modern rebirth driven by small family estates. A warming climate has made ripening far more dependable than it once was, encouraging steady new planting.

name: Slovakia
description:
**Slovakia** is a landlocked Central European country whose vineyards, tucked mostly into its warmer southern belt, turn out predominantly crisp white wines and a growing volume of characterful reds. Long overshadowed by neighbouring Austria and Hungary, it is quietly building a reputation among curious drinkers.

**Signature wines** — Aromatic, dry-to-off-dry whites lead the way, especially Grüner Veltliner, Welschriesling (locally Rizling vlašský), Riesling and Pinot Blanc. Among reds, the Blaufränkisch grape (Frankovka modrá) and St. Laurent (Svätovavrinecké) give juicy, spicy bottles.

**Key regions** — Six official wine regions run across the south, the best known being the Malokarpatská (Small Carpathians) belt near Bratislava, plus Nitra, Southern Slovakia, Central Slovakia and Eastern Slovakia. A small slice of the famous Tokaj sweet-wine zone also lies on the Slovak side of the border with Hungary.

**Good to know** — For much of the 20th century Slovakia was part of Czechoslovakia, and its modern wine industry has been reshaped since independence in 1993 and EU membership. Its Tokaj wines follow rules closely aligned with the shared Hungarian appellation.

name: Ukraine
description:
**Ukraine** is a large Eastern European country with a long viticultural history centred on the warmer lands near the Black Sea, best known for sparkling and sweet dessert wines alongside a growing wave of modern dry table wines.

**Signature wines** — Traditional-method and tank-method sparkling wines are a hallmark, as are rich fortified and dessert styles in the southern coastal zones. A new generation of producers now makes dry whites and reds from both international grapes and regional varieties.

**Key regions** — Viticulture concentrates around the Black Sea coast, notably the Odessa and Kherson areas, with the Crimean peninsula (home to the historic Massandra winery) long celebrated for fortified and dessert wines. The Zakarpattia (Transcarpathia) region in the far west offers a cooler, more Central European style.

**Good to know** — Ukrainian winemaking stretches back to ancient Greek colonies on the Black Sea and was heavily industrialised in the Soviet era, when large state cellars supplied sparkling wine across the USSR. In recent years smaller, quality-focused wineries have driven a revival of the country's dry-wine scene.

name: Uruguay
description:
**Uruguay** is a small but ambitious South American wine country whose cool, humid, Atlantic-influenced climate sets it apart from its bigger neighbours. Though modest in size, it has earned a quality reputation that belies its scale and become almost synonymous with a single grape.

**Signature wines** — Tannat is the national flagship, giving deeply coloured, firmly structured reds that are often rounder and more approachable here than in its French homeland. Uruguay also does well with Albariño, which suits the maritime climate, plus Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Tannat-based blends.

**Key regions** — Most vineyards cluster in the south near the capital, especially Canelones and Montevideo, with Maldonado on the Atlantic coast emerging as a cooler, more artisanal zone.

**Good to know** — Tannat arrived in the 19th century with Basque immigrants, who called it "Harriague" after the settler who introduced it. The country is one of South America's smaller producers by volume, and its wine culture leans toward family-run estates and export-minded, food-friendly styles rather than mass production.

name: Kosovo
description:
**Kosovo** is a small Balkan country with a modest but historically rooted wine industry, concentrated in its warmer, sheltered valleys. Its output is little seen internationally but has a loyal regional following.

**Signature wines** — Production spans both red and white wines, drawing on international varieties such as Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon alongside grapes common across the wider Balkans. Reds have traditionally been the backbone of the industry.

**Key regions** — The main winemaking area lies in the south and west around the town of Rahovec (Orahovac), the heart of Kosovo's vineyards.

**Good to know** — During the Yugoslav era, Kosovo's cooperatives produced large volumes of red wine, much of it exported to Germany under a well-known branded label. Since then the sector has been rebuilding on a smaller, more quality-conscious scale.

name: Latvia
description:
**Latvia** is a Baltic country on the far northern fringe of the wine world, where a cold climate makes conventional grape growing marginal. Its drinks culture leans more toward fruit wines and spirits than classic grape wine, though small-scale viticulture is slowly emerging.

**Signature wines** — Fruit and berry wines are the traditional strength, made from produce such as rhubarb, apples and black currants. A handful of growers now experiment with cold-hardy hybrid grape varieties suited to short northern summers.

**Key regions** — Vineyard activity is scattered and small, with the town of Sabile long noted for a historic hillside vineyard often cited among the more northerly open-air plantings in Europe.

**Good to know** — Latvia is far better known internationally for Riga Black Balsam, a dark herbal liqueur, than for grape wine. Its emerging wine scene is a niche, hobbyist pursuit rather than a commercial industry.
